was enough.
King Kong built hundreds.

The single landing page was a real idea that worked for a specific reason in a specific era. Today it is the comfort blanket that keeps most small businesses invisible in search. Here is where the idea came from, when it still makes sense, and why every business fighting to rank for their own name in 2026 needs to build an authority network — not a homepage.

// The King Kong footer

Scroll to the bottom of kingkong.co and you will find something most visitors never read. Hundreds of links. Birmingham SEO Agency. Seattle SEO Agency. Los Angeles SEO Agency. Every major US city, every state, two service lines — SEO and social media — each combination a separate page. That is not a directory. That is not padding. That is the most deliberate search architecture in the digital marketing industry, sitting in plain sight at the bottom of a homepage most people abandon after reading the first paragraph.

King Kong is an Australian-founded digital marketing agency valued at hundreds of millions. They did not get there with a homepage and a contact form. They got there by building an authority network so dense that when anyone in any US city types "SEO agency [city name]" into Google, there is a reasonable chance a King Kong page is somewhere on that results page.

That strategy has a name, a history, and a version that works for every business — including a panel beater in Goodwood, a bookkeeper in Century City, and a web development agency in Cape Town. The name of the one-page website is not simplicity. It is invisibility.

Where the single landing page actually came from

// Chapter 01 — A real idea for a specific era

The single landing page has a legitimate origin. It was not invented by people who did not understand websites. It was invented by people who understood paid advertising extremely well.

In the early 2000s, Google AdWords changed everything about how businesses reached customers online. For the first time, you could pay to appear at the top of search results for a specific query — and you only paid when someone clicked. The question became: where do you send that click?

The answer, discovered through testing, was not the homepage. When someone clicked an ad for "plumber Cape Town" and landed on a homepage that also talked about electrical work, roofing, and the company's 1987 founding story — they left. When they landed on a page that said "emergency plumber in Cape Town — call now" with nothing else on it — they converted. The single-purpose landing page, stripped of navigation, stripped of distractions, optimised for one action, outperformed a full website for paid traffic consistently.

That finding was real, was documented, and launched an entire industry of landing page builders, A/B testing platforms, and conversion rate optimisation agencies. It was also completely specific to paid traffic — and that specificity got lost.

The mistake that followed: The landing page insight spread from paid advertising to web design as a general principle. "Keep it simple." "One clear message." "Remove distractions." All correct for a paid traffic funnel. Completely counterproductive for organic search. Nobody told most small business owners that the rules were different depending on where the traffic was coming from — and so an entire generation of SA businesses ended up with single-page websites wondering why Google could not find them.

Why a one-page website is invisible in organic search

// Chapter 02 — One page, one keyword, one problem

Google ranks pages, not websites. That is the first thing to understand. When someone searches for something, Google finds the individual page most relevant to that search and returns it. Your homepage competes for whatever keyword it targets. If your homepage says "Cape Town web development agency," it can potentially rank for that phrase. It cannot also rank for "custom SaaS development South Africa" and "business automation Cape Town" and "website developer Milnerton" and "GEO optimisation Cape Town" — because those are four different searches and you have one page.

Every search query you want to be found for requires a page that specifically addresses it. Not mentions it in passing — specifically addresses it, with content that answers the search intent, with a title tag that includes the keyword, with schema markup that tells Google's crawlers what the page is about, with internal links connecting it to related content on your domain.

// One page website
Ranks for 1–3 keywords
  • Only your homepage competes in search
  • Cannot target location-specific searches
  • Cannot target service-specific searches
  • No internal link structure to build authority
  • No topical depth signal for Google
  • Invisible for every question your customer asks
  • Cannot recover if homepage ranking drops
  • Zero content for AI models to cite
// Authority network
Ranks for hundreds of keywords
  • Every page is a new entry point from search
  • Location pages target suburb-level searches
  • Service pages target intent-specific searches
  • Internal links distribute authority across all pages
  • Topical depth signals domain expertise to Google
  • Articles answer the questions your customers search
  • Multiple entry points — one page dropping does not kill rankings
  • Rich content for AI models to cite and surface

// Chapter 03 — Six sitemaps, thousands of pages

King Kong does not have a sitemap. They have six of them. Each one covers a different category of pages — posts, main pages, categories, tags, review types, locales. The locales sitemap alone covers their location-specific pages: every US city, every state, two service lines, hundreds of combinations.

Each of those city pages says approximately the same thing — "we are a [service] agency serving [city]" — with local detail added. Each one targets a specific search query: "SEO agency Birmingham," "social media marketing Portland," "digital marketing agency Nashville." Someone searches. Google finds the relevant page. King Kong gets the click.

This is not spam. This is not keyword stuffing. Each page has genuine content, genuine contact information, and a genuine offer. The model is systematic targeting of every search query your business could plausibly answer — and building a page for each one.

You are not fighting for clicks. You are fighting for your own name. And your name only appears when you have built enough pages to be findable for the searches that lead to it.

The baby seat example — and why it works for every business

// Chapter 04 — The connection is the content

Here is the idea that makes authority networks work for businesses that do not have hundreds of service lines or dozens of cities to target. You do not have to only publish content about your core service. You have to publish content about everything your customer cares about that connects to what you sell.

You sell baby products. Your core customer is a parent — probably a new one, overwhelmed, researching everything, trusting nothing, searching obsessively. They search for car seat safety. They search for which pram fits in a Toyota Yaris. They search for what to do when a toddler refuses the car seat. They search for the best routes from Cape Town to Hermanus with a baby. None of those searches lead to your product page — unless you built content that answers them.

Write the article about car seat safety statistics in South Africa. Cite the road accident data. Explain what a five-star NCAP rating means. Describe the difference between rear-facing and forward-facing installation. At the end — naturally, without a hard sell — the baby seat you stock is the one that meets every criterion you just explained. The customer who read the article trusts you. They already know you know what you are talking about. The conversion is almost incidental.

// Example: baby seat retailer authority network — pages that all lead back to one product
If you sell baby seats, these are the pages that make you findable
Car seat safety South Africa NCAP rating baby seat explained Rear-facing vs forward-facing car seat Best car seat for Toyota Yaris How to install isofix correctly Baby seat laws South Africa 2026 Road trip Cape Town with toddler When to move from baby seat to booster Car seat expiry date — do they expire? Accident — can I reuse a car seat? Baby seat for Uber South Africa legal Buy baby seat Cape Town

Every one of those pages is a question a parent in South Africa types into Google. Every one of them can be answered with genuine, useful content. Every one of them can link back to your product page. None of them are dishonest or manipulative. They are just content that connects the thing you sell to the full context in which someone would need to buy it.

This is not a new strategy. It is the oldest content marketing insight there is — be the most useful thing in your customer's search results, not just when they are ready to buy, but throughout the entire decision-making process. What is new is how accessible it has become. You do not need a content team. You do not need an agency. You need a clear understanding of what your customer searches for and the discipline to keep building.

When the single landing page still makes sense

// Chapter 05 — Context is everything

Before burying the single landing page entirely — it still has its place. For paid advertising campaigns, the conversion-optimised single-purpose page still outperforms a full website. If you are running Google Ads or Meta campaigns and sending traffic to your homepage, you are wasting money. A dedicated landing page for each campaign, with the specific offer, specific call to action, and no navigation to distract — that is still the right architecture for paid traffic.

Event-specific campaigns — a product launch, a sale period, a specific promotion — work well with single landing pages. Early-stage businesses testing a concept before investing in full infrastructure. Products with such a simple value proposition that one clear page communicates everything. Pre-launch waitlists.

The error is using the landing page as a permanent homepage and expecting organic search results from it. These are two different tools for two different jobs. Most South African businesses have a single-page website and zero paid advertising — which means they have the worst possible combination: the architecture that works for paid traffic, applied to a context where they get no paid traffic.

The three rules for building your own authority network

// Chapter 06 — Keep it simple, keep it consistent
01
Every page faces one keyword
Before you write a word, know what search query this page is for. "Website developer Cape Town" is a keyword. "Cape Town web development" is a keyword. "Custom website development Cape Town small business" is a keyword. Write the page for that search. Put it in the title tag, the heading, the first paragraph, the schema markup. One page, one primary keyword, built to answer the intent behind that search.
02
Schema uses the same keywords the content does
Structured data schema is the machine-readable version of your page. The keywords in your visible content must match the keywords in your schema. If your page targets "panel beaters Goodwood Cape Town" then your LocalBusiness schema name, description, and areaServed must say Goodwood and Cape Town. The schema is not decoration — it is the signal that tells Google's AI what your page is actually about, independent of how any human reads the text.
03
Never stop building
An authority network is never finished. King Kong has hundreds of pages and they are still updating them — the page-sitemap was last updated 28 September 2026. Every new page is a new entry point. Every new article is a new keyword you can rank for. Every new connection between pages strengthens the authority of your whole domain. The businesses that dominate their category in South African search started building before their competitors and never stopped. The ones who will dominate in two years are building now.

The South African context — a gap most businesses are not filling

// Chapter 07 — The competitive advantage sitting unclaimed

The authority network strategy is well-understood in the US, UK, and Australia — King Kong is Australian. It is significantly less practiced in South Africa, where the digital marketing conversation is still largely about Facebook ads, social media posting frequency, and whether to use WordPress or Wix.

That gap is the opportunity. The SA business that builds a genuine authority network in their industry — with well-structured pages, proper schema markup, consistent content production, and internal linking — is going to rank above competitors who are relying on a homepage and a prayer. Not because the strategy is secret. Because the strategy requires consistent effort over months, and most businesses stop before the results arrive.
